items.title: Building Ungameable Trust Networks for Curated Directories: Decentralized Filtering Without Central Authority
items.abstract: Search and discovery on the 2026 internet is broken for three groups: users who want to find real businesses and resources, small businesses who want to be found, and honest affiliate operators who want to earn from genuine recommendations. Search engines rank results by signals that reward scale, not quality. A local hardware store cannot outrank a content farm that produces ten thousand SEO-optimized pages per day with large language models. Paying for search advertising puts small businesses into bidding wars against companies with orders-of-magnitude larger budgets. Social media demands constant content production — videos, posts, engagement farming — work that has nothing to do with the actual service the business provides. Review platforms are corrupted. Fake reviews, review bombing, pay-to-play visibility schemes, and extortion dynamics have made star ratings unreliable. Users append "reddit" to their search queries as a trust signal, but Reddit itself is degrading as it monetizes and as marketers infiltrate communities. AI answer engines attempt to solve the problem by synthesizing responses, but they draw from the same polluted index and introduce hallucination risk. The underlying data is compromised. No amount of summarization fixes a contaminated source. Honest affiliate operators face the same structural disadvantage. An operator who genuinely tests products and recommends what they believe in cannot compete on volume against content farms that rewrite product descriptions and stuff affiliate links without touching the products. The algorithm cannot distinguish the two. The content farm wins on output volume every time. Three intermediaries sit between a person and a useful resource: algorithmic ranking that rewards manipulation, centralized moderation that makes uniform visibility decisions for all users, and review systems that are themselves a manipulation surface. All three are failing.

items.title: Can Machines Perform Emotional Labor in Education? Tracing Debates in Early Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI) system perform the emotional labor of teaching, or can it only reproduce emotional labor's outward signs? In this article, I argue that the latter does not by itself justify the former. Emotional labor in education includes surface acting, but it still presupposes an agent capable of emotion, self‐regulation, and responsibility within a pedagogical relation. Its educational value can also depend on students' reasonable perception that care is not wholly fabricated. I develop this claim through selected debates about machinic emotion from 1950 to 1996. Ziff, Smart, and Putnam dispute whether feeling requires biological life or can be attributed through organized behavior; Weiss, Scriven, and Danto test whether relation, honesty, and language can evidence machine emotion; and Dyer, Ortony et al., and Arbib contest whether computational appraisal can capture embodied affect. These debates do not supply a historical test that contemporary systems must pass. They expose three still‐relevant justificatory questions about ontology, evidence, and embodiment that divide educational critics and technologists. This article uses those questions to distinguish computational representations and simulations of emotion from warranted claims that a system has emotion and performs emotional labor. The result is a shared vocabulary for evaluating affective AI in education and for identifying which forms of pedagogical care cannot simply be inferred from emotionally convincing output.

items.title: Challenges of Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education – A Brief Literature Review
items.abstract: The world economy is in the era of the fourth industrial revolution and digital transformation, which has and will continue to affect all spheres of human life. The invention of artificial intelligence (AI) is the result of the above-mentioned process, and it is important to know how to use it correctly. On the one hand, if employers require employees to use various artificial intelligence programs, there is heated discussion in educational institutions about students' improper use of these tools, which leads to a decrease in critical and analytical thinking among young people. It is worth noting that world-renowned universities are seeking to adopt internal regulations on the use of artificial intelligence independently; however, it is important to strike a balance that ensures the training of highly qualified, analytical, and critical-thinking students while equipping them with the technological skills necessary for employment. Research on this topic at various universities worldwide shows that the use of artificial intelligence is effective in some courses, such as English-as-a-foreign-language instruction. However, in preparing a master's or doctoral thesis, which must be original research based on conclusions formulated by the student, the intensive use of AI will not have the desired effect. It is noteworthy that Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University has developed an AI Strategy 2026-2029, within the framework of which the results of the survey of teachers and employers conducted coincide with the conclusions of similar studies conducted abroad. items.title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
items.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3×, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20–30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

items.abstract: This record contains the English translation of sustentabilidade cognitiva — Interação Humano-Máquina, version 1.0, originally published in Portuguese on 31 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23846541. The translation was prepared with artificial intelligence assistance on 1 November 2026. This is a theoretical-conceptual preprint and has not undergone peer review. This article presents the conceptual architecture of cognitive sustainability in Human–Machine Interaction developed within the QU and QUEaSTION programme. The guiding question is how intelligibility, autonomy and the conditions for recognition can be preserved when people and systems participate in addressing a dilemma. The approach connects an author-created map of the cognitive process with the current programme manuscripts and selected literature on automation and interaction. The account relates dilemmas, areas of life, roles, actors, SER–TER–ESTAR (being, having and situated states), field influences, preservation, prioritisation, recognisable capacities, applied skills, memories, permission, action and outcomes. It defines QU as the semantic organisation of capacities recognised when weighing dilemmas in complex systems and explains the role of the SEM framework in preserving the meanings being compared. It presents state transformations, the PAC, PAI and PIR patterns, and the distinction between Projected Outcome, Expected Outcome and Produced Outcome. QUEaSTION supports the traceable reconstruction of these relationships; QUIA constitutes a line of technical development. A fictional example of digital scheduling illustrates the scope of the proposal. The contribution consists in organising the framework and delimiting questions for further conceptual development and subsequent empirical investigations.

items.title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Financial Performance: The Mediating Role of Employee Engagement and the Moderating Role of Job Autonomy in Malaysian Manufacturing Firms
items.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has historically been treated as a discretionary activity outside the realm of strategic management. However, over time CSR has gained traction as a necessary addition to any organisation with positive impact on the firm’s bottom line. Despite this progress, how CSR affects financial performance is not well understood, especially in an emerging- market manufacturing setting. This study investigates CSR’s impact on financial performance for Malaysian manufacturing firms while testing employee engagement as a mediating variable and job autonomy as a moderating condition. Five hypotheses were formulated on the basis of Stakeholder Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory; direct effects of CSR on employee engagement and financial performance, the indirect effect of employee engagement on financial performance, mediation of employee engagement, and moderation of job autonomy were investigated. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was utilised. Participants were Malaysian employees working in manufacturing firms who completed a questionnaire. 384 completed questionnaires were collected from a sample of 500 resulting in a response rate of 76.8%. Data were analysed through descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and conditional process analysis with PROCESS Model 7 using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results found CSR to have a positive and significant effect on financial performance and employee engagement. Employee engagement had a positive and significant effect on financial performance and fully mediated the relationship between CSR and financial performance. Job autonomy was found to have no significant effect on the relationship between CSR and employee engagement but was found to have a positive and significant relationship with employee engagement. This study contributes to the field of CSR by providing evidence that employee engagement serves as an important internal mechanism through which responsible organisational practices affect financial performance. The findings of this study show that job design may play an important role in manufacturing contexts where there are more formal procedures and requirements for operation.

items.title: DECODING FEEDBACK: HOW STUDENTS’ CONCEPTIONS OF FEEDBACK DRIVE COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effect of students’ conceptions of feedback on their cognitive engagement. Although student cognitive engagement is an extensively researched construct, it is still developing, and various areas remain to be explored one of which is the assessment context for student engagement. Educational researchers have highlighted that investigating the relationship between assessment and student engagement is crucial. To collect data for the constructs, a survey methodology was employed using a convenience sample of 499 university students from six public and private institutions. Two validated instruments the Students’ Conceptions of Feedback (SCoF) inventory and Cognitive Engagement sub-scales from Attitudes Towards Mathematics (ATM) were administered after obtaining formal permission from the developers. Hypotheses were derived from an extensive literature review. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 3 was utilized for statistical analysis. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive effect of SCoF on cognitive engagement.

items.title: Designing an Artificial Intelligence–Based Cognitive Empowerment Package to Enhance Entrepreneurial Skills in Gifted and Creative Adolescents
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

items.title: Designing and Explaining an Entrepreneurship Model for Artificial Intelligence–Based Businesses
items.abstract: The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

items.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies is transforming modern economies by creating new mechanisms of production, distribution, consumption, and public administration. This article examines the theoretical foundations and current trends of the digital economy, focusing on the experience of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Particular attention is given to the "Digital Uzbekistan – 2030" strategy, digital infrastructure, e-government, digital finance, e-commerce, the IT sector, and human capital development. The study applies systematic, comparative, and institutional approaches, as well as the analysis of statistical and regulatory information. The findings show that Uzbekistan has established important institutional and technological foundations for digital transformation. However, challenges remain, including the digital divide, a shortage of qualified specialists, cybersecurity risks, unequal regional access to digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The study proposes strengthening digital infrastructure, developing digital skills, expanding the application of artificial intelligence and big data, supporting digital entrepreneurship, and promoting international digital integration. items.title: Does Informal Digital Learning of English Work Through Feelings or Through Traits? A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Affective and Individual-Difference Pathways
items.abstract: Informal digital learning of English (IDLE) — learners' self-organized engagement with English through short videos, social media, streaming, gaming, and generative AI outside the classroom — has accumulated a large body of empirical research over the past decade, yet its affective and individual-difference correlates have never been quantitatively synthesized. Existing meta-analyses address only overall effects on achievement, and narrative reviews of emotion and individual-difference variables have pooled no effect sizes. This preregistration reports a three-level meta-analysis that (1) estimates the strength of association between IDLE and positive emotions, negative emotions, and individual-difference variables; (2) tests whether the association with positive emotions is stronger than that with negative emotions, as predicted by broaden-and-build and control-value theories; and (3) explores whether the affective pathway is conditional on trait-like individual differences. Ten sources (Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, OpenAlex, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, CNKI, Scopus) will be searched for correlational studies published from 2014 onward. Effect sizes (Pearson's r, Fisher's z-transformed) will be modeled with three-level random-effects models cross-validated by cluster-robust variance estimation, with seven prespecified moderators and publication-bias correction (PET-PEESE). Expected outcomes are the first preregistered, effect-size-level synthesis of the IDLE–affect/individual-difference literature, clarifying whether IDLE works through feelings or through traits.

items.title: Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation
items.abstract: Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation extends the Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) framework by examining how personalization, trust, human agency, and boundaries should develop together in adaptive AI experiences. As AI systems become increasingly personalized, usefulness depends not only on what an AI system learns about an individual, but also on understanding what information should not be disclosed, reused, inferred, or carried into another context. This paper introduces Progressive Boundary Formation as a human-centered process through which individuals can recognize, communicate, test, and revise personal, relational, professional, and organizational boundaries as their interaction with AI develops. The framework considers the transition from private AI-assisted exploration to consequential human action, including communication, publication, professional activity, and interactions involving other people. It proposes that boundary awareness should develop alongside personalization and trust rather than appearing only as a static privacy setting or late-stage safeguard. Progressive Boundary Formation is presented as a conceptual extension of Dynamic PGA and its broader goal of creating AI experiences that adapt with the human while preserving human judgment, agency, relationships, and appropriate boundaries. items.title: EFL Students’ Experiences with AI-Powered Language Learning Tools: Implications for Learner-Centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into English language learning through tools that provide adaptive learning, automated feedback, and personalized support. Although previous studies have examined the educational benefits of AI-powered tools, relatively little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students experience these technologies and how their perspectives can inform the design of learner-centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). This study explored EFL students’ experiences, perceived benefits, challenges, and expectations regarding AI-powered tools for English language learning. A qualitative research design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with nine Vietnamese university EFL students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that participants experienced AI-powered language learning tools as adaptive, feedback-oriented, and engaging. They particularly valued immediate feedback, flexible learning opportunities, and gamified features, which they associated with greater confidence, motivation, and learner autonomy. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, the contextual and cultural appropriateness of AI-generated feedback, and data privacy and security. Participants also envisioned future ITS as more conversational, personalized, and culturally responsive systems that could better address individual learning needs. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed AI as a valuable learning support while emphasizing the importance of independent learning, teacher guidance, and contextual relevance. The study offers preliminary design implications for learner-centered ITS by highlighting the importance of incorporating learners’ experiences and expectations into future AI-supported language learning systems.

items.title: Enhancing Clinical Reasoning Development: An AI-Assisted Learning Framework for Unstructured Problem-Solving in Medical Education
items.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical reasoning for unstructured problems—those lacking clearly defined initial conditions, standard protocols, or singular correct solutions—remains a persistent challenge in medical education. While artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in structured knowledge tasks, their integration into frameworks designed for unstructured clinical reasoning remains underexplored. Methods A systems thinking assessment framework was adapted for medical education and validated through expert review and inter-rater reliability testing (ICC = 0.801, 95% CI: 0.725–0.866). Fifty-five medical students were randomly assigned to three groups: an AI-assisted learning group (AIL, n = 18) using ChatGPT 4.0 as a guided reasoning aid, a conventional learning group (CL, n = 18) using textbooks and non-AI online resources, and a manual group (MG, n = 19) without any supplementary tools. All participants responded to the same unstructured clinical case comprising seven tasks (Q1–Q7), each scored on a 0–3 scale by five blinded raters. As an exploratory benchmark, ChatGPT 4.0 responses to the identical case were independently scored using the same framework to characterize the AI model's performance profile and limitations. Results The AIL group achieved the highest mean total score (12.11 ± 1.78), significantly outperforming the CL group (8.94 ± 1.08, p < 0.0001) and the MG (9.97 ± 2.37, p < 0.01). Significant advantages were observed in Q2 (information needs), Q5 (scenario development), Q6 (challenges), and Q7 (unintended consequences). Subgroup analysis revealed no significant interaction between learning tools and baseline academic performance (F = 0.213, p = 0.930, η² = 0.018), suggesting consistent benefits across GPA levels. The ChatGPT 4.0 benchmark produced uniformly identical scores (total score 16.5 across all trials), revealing characteristic limitations in response variability and template dependency. Conclusions An AI-assisted learning framework grounded in a validated systems thinking assessment tool can enhance medical students' clinical reasoning for unstructured problems, with effects that appear independent of baseline academic performance. The ChatGPT benchmark highlights both the capabilities and the rigidities of current AI models, underscoring the need for hybrid human–AI collaboration rather than AI substitution in clinical reasoning education. items.title: ETHICAL AND REGULATORY COMPLIANCE IN THE EVALUATION OF CLINICAL RESEARCH INVOLVING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN SUB SAHARAN AFRICA
items.abstract: In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

items.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
items.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

items.title: Factors Affecting the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Among Librarians in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Librarians' readiness for metaverse technology in Nigerian universities of technology is not well documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Methods This cross-sectional survey was conducted between April and July 2026 in six Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria. Academic librarians in these universities who agreed to participate were included, and incomplete questionnaires were excluded. Data were collected with a validated online questionnaire using four-point scales. Descriptive statistics were used with a criterion mean of 2.50, and Pearson correlation was used to test the hypotheses at a 0.05 significance level. Results A total of 103 librarians were included. Overall, 97 (94.2%) reported very high or high awareness of the metaverse concept. While 91 (88.3%) reported being able to operate metaverse access devices, 29 (28.2%) reported being able to upload library content. Reliable internet connectivity was reported by 87 (84.5%), and augmented reality devices by 27 (26.2%). Inadequate training was the most highly rated challenge, reported by 98 (95.1%). Awareness was correlated with digital skills (r = 0.49, p < 0.001), and infrastructure with organizational support (r = 0.38, p < 0.001). Conclusion Librarians appeared to be aware of metaverse technology, but their skills and resources seemed better suited to accessing virtual environments than to delivering library services within them. Introduction The metaverse refers to a persistent, shared multiuser virtual environment that merges physical reality with digital virtuality, in which users interact with one another and with digital content through avatars, supported by virtual, augmented, and mixed reality technologies [1]. The term originated in the 1992 science fiction novel Snow Crash, and the concept has since attracted substantial attention from technology companies and researchers [1,2]. In academic libraries, metaverse technologies have been applied or proposed for virtual tours, exhibitions, information literacy instruction, access to digital collections, and interaction between librarians and users [3,4]. Librarians' awareness of and readiness for metaverse technology have been examined in Thailand, the Gulf region, the United States, and Nigeria [5–8]. Factors reported to influence adoption include librarians' awareness and digital competence; the availability of devices, software, bandwidth, and electricity; and organizational support in the form of funding, training, technical assistance, and policy [9,10]. Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity have also been identified as implementation concerns [11]. In Nigeria, studies of university libraries have reported variation in digital competencies and technological resources, and interest in metaverse applications alongside limitations in expertise, infrastructure, funding, training, and policy [8,12]. Federal Universities of Technology hold a mandate for technological education and research; however, librarians' awareness, digital skills, and perceptions of infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges relating to metaverse technology in these institutions remain insufficiently documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Literature Review Awareness of Metaverse Technology among Librarians Proposed library applications of metaverse technology include immersive user engagement and changes to collections and reading spaces [3,13]; virtual, augmented, and mixed reality services [14]; virtual tours, simulations, tutorials, and collaborative spaces [4]; and immersive information literacy instruction [15]. From the user perspective, studies have examined willingness to patronise a metaverse academic library [16], intentions to use metaverse digital library services [17], knowledge exchange through a virtual living library [18], and information needs involving interaction, participation, and user-generated content in metaverse communities [19]. Among librarians, moderate awareness has been reported in Thailand [5] and in Nigeria, where it was accompanied by enthusiasm for adoption [12]. However, the relationship between librarians' awareness and their digital skills has not been examined in Nigerian Federal Universities of Technology. Digital Skills Possessed by Librarians for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology New professional capabilities have been described as necessary for librarians in intelligent library environments [20]. Librarians in the Gulf region have reported substantial familiarity with and interest in metaverse technology, together with barriers related to expertise and technical resources [6]. Positive views of metaverse integration have also been reported alongside gaps in technical expertise [21]. In Nigeria, digital skills have been associated with preparedness for metaverse-enabled services [12], and readiness and digital capacity have been reported to vary across universities [8]. Training has been recommended to address these gaps [4,10,22]. However, existing studies have not distinguished librarians' ability to navigate virtual environments from their ability to create content, retrieve resources, and communicate with users within them. Adequacy of Technological Infrastructure for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Infrastructure has been identified as a factor in the adoption of metaverse technologies in academic libraries [9] and has been associated with readiness among library professionals in Pakistan [23]. Immersive library applications and scalable metaverse service models require high-capacity connectivity, and internet and infrastructure constraints have been identified as barriers to implementation [4,14]. Reviews of metaverse technologies in libraries have also highlighted implementation constraints [10,22]. In Nigeria, studies have reported uneven technological resources and limited institutional readiness [8,12]. In a related context, facilitating conditions have been associated with librarians' adoption of artificial intelligence [24]. Organizational Support Available for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Institutional encouragement has been linked with favorable perceptions of metaverse technology among librarians [6], and leadership support has been identified as a component of readiness in Pakistan [23]. In urban libraries in the United States, overall operating expenditure and population served did not explain the application of metaverse-related technologies [7]. In Nigeria, financial and policy constraints have been reported [12]. Recommended measures include professional development [20]; phased implementation, training, and user feedback [4]; and collaboration, policy, and investment [10,22]. Challenges Affecting the Adoption of Metaverse Technology among Librarians. Reported barriers include technical, financial, and ethical concerns in Thailand [5]; connectivity, training, and service delivery [4]; resource and inclusion issues [10,22]; and costs, skills, funding, and readiness in Nigeria [12]. Professional challenges include changes to librarians' roles [20] and changes associated with the convergence of metaverse technology and artificial intelligence [25]. Ethical and security concerns have also been identified [5,22], including cybersecurity and data protection [11]. At the service level, challenges relate to community participation and ownership of information [19] and to the transfer of knowledge exchange into virtual settings [18]. items.title: GenAI Frontline Workers and Sociotechnical Governance: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: This study conducts a systematic literature review, following the PRISMA 2020 protocol across Scopus and Web of Science, yielding 36 articles.It examined how GenAI integration in frontline service operations redefines task automation boundaries, reconfigures work and competency demands, and gives rise to new sociotechnical governance arrangements.The findings reveal that GenAI dissolves the classical routine/non-routine boundary established by Autor et al. (2003), entering cognitive and socio-emotional service interaction domains, with automation operating along a complexity-determined gradient formalized through the Switch Point concept.A structural upskilling-deskilling paradox emerges simultaneously: while GenAI improves service outcomes and generates new competency demandssuch as prompt engineering or AI trainersit can erode domain expertise through overreliance across healthcare, financial services, education, and hospitality contexts.Addressing this tension requires governance at three interdependent levels: operational (HITL configurations and RAG-anchored systems), organizational (AI Teams and new professional roles), and institutional (Corporate Digital Responsibility frameworks).Collectively, these findings contribute a gradient conception of automation boundaries, consolidate the upskilling-deskilling tension as a structural cross-sectoral phenomenon, and propose a three-level governance architecture for frontline service delivery.Competitive advantage stems not from GenAI adoption per se, but from the organizational capability to configure and govern human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Generative AI and Composing Strategies Employed by EFL Writers: Is AI a Double-edged Sword?
items.abstract: The integration of AI tools like ChatGPT in language education presents both opportunities and challenges. This mixed-methods study examined the impact of AI on composing strategies and writing performance among 87 upper-intermediate Iranian EFL learners, randomly assigned to a traditional group (n=43) and an AI group (n=44). Both groups completed IELTS Writing Task 2 as pre- and post-tests; the AI group used ChatGPT during the post-test. Concurrent think-aloud protocols, supported by training and video demonstrations, were used to analyze writing strategies, while reflective journals provided qualitative insights. Results showed the AI group achieved significantly higher post-test scores but employed fewer cognitive, rhetorical, metacognitive, communicative, and socio-affective writing strategies, indicating reduced strategic engagement. Thematic analysis revealed learners’ ambivalence: they valued AI for efficiency and personalized feedback but expressed concerns about authenticity, creativity, equity, and academic integrity. The findings suggest that while AI can enhance writing performance, over-reliance may hinder critical skill development. The study advocates for critical AI literacy, emphasizing scaffolded, ethical AI integration aligned with Vygotskian principles. Educators should prioritize personal voice, originality, and higher-order thinking to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes, the writing process.

items.title: HERMES–AEGIS: AI-assisted security for operational technology with structural separation from the plant
items.abstract: HERMES–AEGIS is a research programme on AI assistance for security teams in industrial plants and other critical infrastructure. It rests on three principles. First, separation by structure: no component that reads AI output is given credentials or a network path to controllers or safety systems, with the plant boundary enforced one way. Second, evidence before conclusions: every claim is tied to its source data and checked before an analyst sees it. Third, intelligence by need: each step uses the least costly sufficient AI model and escalates only when the evidence calls for it. This note sets out the problem, the principles and the current status. HERMES, the reasoning layer, exists as a research prototype exercised with simulated models; AEGIS, a read-only incident-triage application for OT security teams, is in preparation. The note includes one observational result from 7,366 public AI-agent task recordings. It is not a product announcement, makes no claim of validation against real incidents, and makes no claim of compliance with ISA/IEC 62443, NIST guidance or any regulation.

items.title: Hubungan antara Penggunaan AI dalam Pembelajaran dan Motivasi Belajar Mahasiswa Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar
items.abstract: The expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning has the potential to support students’ learning processes, but its relationship with learning motivation among Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar (PGSD) students still requires investigation. This study aims to analyze the relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students. The study employed a quantitative approach with a correlational design involving 38 PGSD students. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Pearson’s product–moment correlation test with SPSS. The results showed a positive and significant relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students, with a relatively weak correlation (r = 0.352; p = 0.030). Students with higher levels of AI use tended to have higher learning motivation, but this relationship did not indicate causality. This study concludes that AI use in learning is associated with learning motivation among PGSD students. These findings add empirical evidence to research on AI use and learning motivation and can serve as a reference for students and educators in using AI wisely and responsibly as a learning aid. Future research should involve more respondents and examine other factors associated with students’ learning motivation.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Finance and Decision Making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in financial services for fraud detection, credit assessment, investment support and digital banking, yet its adoption depends on how users perceive its benefits, risks and trustworthiness. This study examines user perceptions of artificial intelligence in finance, focusing on perceived benefits, perceived risks, trust, explainability, perceived usefulness, adoption intention and perceived effectiveness of financial decisions. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was used, and primary data were collected from 30 respondents through a structured online questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach alpha reliability analysis and Spearman rank correlation with Holm adjustment for multiple testing were applied. Perceived benefits and perceived usefulness were positively associated with adoption intention, and adoption intention was positively associated with perceived decision effectiveness; all three associations remained significant after adjustment. The expected negative association between perceived risk and adoption intention was not found, and the trust and explainability hypotheses were not supported. Because the sample was small and concentrated among young respondents in information technology occupations, the findings are exploratory and should not be generalized. The results suggest that perceived value is linked with willingness to use artificial intelligence based financial tools, while the roles of trust and risk need further study.

items.title: Instructor Authority and Generative AI in Japanese Writing Instruction
items.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has begun to change writing classrooms in ways that are not always immediately visible. In second language education, students now revise and refine texts through AI-supported interaction before teachers ever see the final product. This shift raises questions not only about writing quality, but also about how teachers understand, evaluate, and guide the writing process itself. In Japanese writing instruction, where revision often depends on close attention to context, nuance, and interpersonal positioning, these changes carry particular weight. This study examines how ten instructors of Japanese writing at Hanoi University perceive the growing presence of generative AI in their teaching. Based on survey data and qualitative interpretation, the analysis shows that writing instruction remains deeply dependent on teacher labor, especially in areas that require contextual judgment and individualized feedback. At the same time, many instructors described a growing sense of uncertainty. When revision happens through AI outside the classroom, it becomes harder to determine what a student can actually do alone, and this weakens confidence in conventional forms of assessment. Some participants also felt that the teacher’s traditional role as the central source of correction is becoming less stable. Yet this did not lead them to view AI as a replacement. Instead, they emphasized that meaning-making in Japanese writing still relies on human sensitivity to social context and rhetorical intention. Rather than simply introducing efficiency, generative AI appears to be changing the balance of authority in writing education itself.

items.abstract: The incorporation of artificial intelligence into accounting activities has generated new possibilities for process automation, information processing, and professional decision-making support. This study aimed to analyze the perception and use of artificial intelligence tools in accounting decision-making among professionals in Guayaquil. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted through a survey administered to professionals working in accounting-related areas. From a population of 307 accountants approached, 222 valid responses were obtained through non-probability convenience sampling. The findings showed that 67.57% of participants considered that artificial intelligence tools improve the accuracy of accounting decisions, while 61.26% reported using them for this type of decision-making. Likewise, 76.58% indicated that these tools reduce the time required to make decisions. A statistically significant association was identified between age and willingness to use artificial intelligence, χ²(3) = 68.63, p < .001, with a Cramer's V of .56. The findings suggest that artificial intelligence has a favorable perception among the professionals studied, although its implementation requires training, human oversight, and ethical criteria.

items.title: ISLAMIC ETHICS AND THE CRISIS OF DIGITAL INTEGRITY: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF TRUTH, DECEPTION AND RESPONSIBILITY IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now produce fluent text, realistic images and convincing audio at almost no cost, and it does so without any commitment to truth. This has created a crisis of digital integrity: fabricated content is hard to distinguish from authentic content, machine outputs present invented claims as fact, and it is unclear who should answer for the resulting harm. Mainstream AI ethics has responded with principles such as transparency and accountability, but these frameworks draw mainly on Western philosophical traditions and treat deception largely as a technical or regulatory problem. Islamic scholarship on AI has grown quickly, yet most of it addresses AI in general through maqasid al-shariah, and its treatment of misinformation relies almost entirely on the receiver's duty of tabayyun (verification). This concept paper critically analyses truth, deception and responsibility in generative AI through Islamic ethics. Using conceptual analysis and theory adaptation, it synthesises the empirical literature on synthetic media with Qur'anic, prophetic and juristic concepts. It argues that Islamic ethics offers an integrated account built on three pillars: sidq (truthfulness) as a duty owed by every speaker and publisher, the prohibition of ghish, tadlis and kadhib (deception, concealment and falsehood) as limits on design and deployment, and amanah and mas'uliyyah (trust and answerability) as a model of responsibility that always returns to a human agent. The paper proposes a Digital Integrity Framework that distributes these duties across developers, deployers, users and regulators, and offers suggestions for policy, education and future research.

items.title: Judgment in AI Policy Advice: Humans-in-the-Loop, Appreciation, and the DOGE Experience
items.abstract: Recent studies of Policy Advisory Systems (PAS) focus on the quality of advice and how it is designed and managed. This article extends this analysis looking at the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on advisory systems’ behaviour and activity using Geoffrey Vickers’ concept of policy judgment. It notes how negligible user costs combined with the apparent robustness of AI computational outputs can generate advice that can exercise an important and independent influence on policy decisions and outcomes, despite that advice not always being accurate or well-considered. In this sense AI-generated advice shares some of the same characteristics of earlier mechanical algorithms framing policy problems and recommendations for action which lack the hallmarks of careful appreciation of the issues at stake. This is illustrated by the use of AI tools by the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in 2025-2026, in particular its directive to autonomously reduce the number and size of contracts and grants made by many Departments, and specifically the US Department of Veterans Affairs. The case underlines that a crucial design challenge for AI-based policy advice is to go beyond only trying to ensure human oversight or a ‘Human-in-the-Loop’ in order to ensure that problems are properly articulated and actions towards them are sound.

items.title: Kemampuan Berpikir Kritis Generasi Z di Era Artificial Intelligence dan Media Sosial: Perspektif Teori Paulo Freire
items.abstract: The presence of artificial intelligence (AI) and social media has transformed Generation Z’s patterns of learning, information seeking, and everyday interaction. However, previous research findings have not yielded consistent conclusions regarding the effects of these two technologies on critical thinking skills, while studies interpreting them through Paulo Freire’s critical education perspective remain limited. This study aims to analyze the partial and simultaneous effects of AI use and social media use intensity on Generation Z’s critical thinking skills and to interpret the results from Paulo Freire’s perspective. The study employed a quantitative approach with an explanatory survey design involving 100 Generation Z respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using an online questionnaire and analyzed through multiple linear regression with the assistance of SPSS. The findings indicate that AI use had no significant partial effect on critical thinking skills (p = 0.416), nor did the intensity of social media use (p = 0.198). Simultaneously, the two variables also had no significant effect on critical thinking skills (p = 0.435) and explained only 1.7% of the variation in these skills (R² = 0.017). These findings are consistent with Paulo Freire’s thought, which positions dialogue, reflection, and praxis as the primary elements in developing critical thinking skills rather than technology alone. This study concludes that AI and social media are not direct determinants of critical thinking skills but rather learning tools whose benefits depend on how users utilize, evaluate, and reflect on information. Theoretically, this study enriches educational research in the digital era by integrating Freire’s critical education perspective. Practically, these findings emphasize the importance of reflective learning, information verification, and dialogical methods in developing Generation Z’s critical thinking skills.

items.title: Leadership Practices and Employee Motivation of Selected Tenant General Contractors in a Medium-Scale Commercial Project: Basis for a Workforce Engagement Program
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between leadership practices and employee motivation among construction workers employed by selected tenant general contractors in a medium-scale commercial project in Santa Rosa, Laguna, Philippines, as a basis for developing a Workforce Engagement Program. Anchored in Full-Range Leadership Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design involving 63 construction workers from five tenant general contractors selected through total enumeration. Data were collected using an expert-validated structured survey questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Pearson product-moment correlation. Findings revealed that most respondents had limited construction experience and relatively short company tenure. Leadership practices were generally perceived positively, with supervisory support receiving the highest weighted mean (3.76), while recognition and appreciation received the lowest (2.82), indicating weaknesses in formal monetary and non-monetary recognition. Employee motivation was generally high, particularly intrinsic motivation (3.72), followed by professional growth (3.58) and extrinsic motivation (3.57). However, the relationship between leadership practices and employee motivation was statistically nonsignificant (r = −0.022, p = 0.864). The study proposed KILOS-KAPWA: A Construction Workforce Engagement and Recognition Program to strengthen supervisory communication, employee recognition, professional development, workplace support, and participatory decision-making. The findings align with Sustainable Development Goal 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure). The proposed program may contribute to organizational and socioeconomic sustainability by supporting workforce engagement, employee development, and responsible construction workforce management, although its effectiveness requires evaluation following implementation.

items.title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Research in Strategic Management: A Bibliometric Analysis and Future Research Agenda
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in strategic decision-making, competitive positioning, innovation management, organizational learning, and governance, yet the literature remains fragmented across management, information systems, innovation, and technology-management fields. This study provides a focused bibliometric review of AI research in strategic management. Scopus was used as the primary database, and the query "artificial intelligence" AND "strategic management" was applied to titles, abstracts, and keywords, with restrictions to Business, Management and Accounting, Article and Review document types, and English-language publications. From 126 retrieved records, relevance screening excluded 82 records, leaving 44 publications for analysis. The study examines annual trends, citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence, country distribution, science maps, TCCM synthesis, and a WoS/SSCI sensitivity analysis. Results show slow development before 2018 and marked acceleration after 2023, with 2026 treated as an incomplete year. Themes are shifting from decision support and strategic planning toward generative AI, innovation management, sustainability, organizational capabilities, and governance. By combining bibliometric mapping, TCCM, and cross-database sensitivity analysis, this study offers a knowledge-structure map and future research agenda.

items.title: Measuring Artificial Intelligence Integration in South African Private Higher Education: Applying a Refined Academic Quality Management Model
items.abstract: This study applies a refined model of Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into Academic Quality Management Systems (AQMS) within South African private higher education. It builds on prior validation through exploratory factor analysis and reliability testing to examine how institutional factors relate to stakeholders’ perceptions of AI integration. Survey data from higher education and education technology stakeholders were analysed using PLS-SEM, correlation, multiple regression, and descriptive statistics. The results show moderate explanatory power, with regression indicating stronger overall model performance than PLS-SEM. Across analyses, Research Governance and Responsible AI Use emerged as the most consistent and statistically supported factor associated with AI_QMS. Strategic Planning and AI in Teaching and Learning also contributed positively, although their effects varied by method. In contrast, AI Literacy and Competency Development and Assessment and Evaluation produced inconsistent results, including negative regression coefficients, which are interpreted cautiously due to shared variance and measurement limitations. Other factors, including Ethical Considerations and Data Privacy, Environmental Impact, and Interdisciplinary Collaboration, did not demonstrate independent explanatory power in multivariable models. The findings highlight that observable institutional activity does not necessarily translate into consistent integration within academic quality systems. The study contributes a multi-dimensional framework that distinguishes between strongly supported relationships, method-dependent effects, and areas requiring further measurement development. Practically, the model provides institutions with a structured approach to assess and strengthen AI integration within academic quality management.

items.title: Motivations and Constraints for Playing Electronic Games: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: The objective of this scoping review was to map the existing scientific literature on the relationship between motivations and constraints for playing digital games and esports, characterizing study profiles, identifying dominant themes and tensions, and examining the extent to which their interaction has been theorized and empirically investigated. Following Arksey and O'Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a search across EBSCO, SCOPUS, and Web of Science identified 38 eligible studies published between 1985 and 2025. The findings reveal a profound structural and theoretical imbalance: research is heavily skewed toward motivation-driven "pull factors" (76.3 %), while constraints remain critically understudied (13.2 %). Crucially, integrative studies (10.5 %) demonstrate that while intrinsic motivations can mitigate logistical barriers, deep psychosocial and symbolic constraints rooted in identity exclusion and social stigma consistently override motivation, triggering disengagement or severe affective costs. This review exposes the theoretical limitations of isolated psychological models, arguing for integrative, socio-culturally sensitive frameworks capable of capturing motivations and constraints as interdependent dynamics of the situated gaming experience.

items.title: On the Issue of International Legal Guarantees for Personal Data Protection in the Context of Hybrid Warfare
items.abstract: This article investigates the complex problem of protecting human personal data during modern armed conflicts, particularly through the prism of hybrid warfare. The rapid pace of digitalization, the advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, and their active integration into the military sphere drive the relevance of this study. These factors cause fundamental changes in the methods and means of warfare, as well as in the very purpose of armed conflict. Today, informational influence and psychological pressure on the enemy's population - which are not always accompanied by a direct armed attack - constitute an integral component of any 21st-century military conflict. Consequently, the study analyzes the concept of hybrid warfare, defining it through characteristic features such as asymmetry, large-scale involvement of non-state actors, latency, and a combination of military and non-military means of struggle. The research specifically focuses on the role of generative artificial intelligence in the context of growing cyber threats. The paper emphasizes that unauthorized access to individuals' personal data during an armed conflict allows opposing parties to exert targeted psychological influence on population groups or individuals, manipulate public opinion through disinformation and «deepfakes,» and apply illegal filtration and terror against the population. Furthermore, this study analyzes the current international legal framework regarding personal data protection in conflict conditions. It examines the provisions of international humanitarian law, particularly the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. The findings establish that IHL norms lack special provisions for protecting digitized information. Moreover, ongoing discussions among researchers regarding the recognition of digital data as a «civilian object» significantly complicate the qualification of an enemy's actions in cyberspace as a violation of international humanitarian law. Finally, the article explores the provisions of specific international acts regulating data protection. The analysis determines that the permitted derogation from certain obligations in this sphere can lead to state abuses, often hidden behind the necessity of ensuring national security and defense. Ultimately, the paper highlights that international human rights law, through the provisions of international treaties and the case law of the ECtHR, establishes general guarantees to ensure compliance with the criteria of legality, strict necessity, and proportionality when interfering with the human right to personal data protection.

items.title: Pengaruh Literasi Digital terhadap Etika Penggunaan Artificial Intelligence pada Mahasiswa Perguruan Tinggi
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has transformed the way students seek information, complete assignments, and understand academic materials. However, AI use also raises ethical issues, including plagiarism, overreliance on instant answers, and a lack of transparency in acknowledging AI assistance. This study aims to analyze the effect of digital literacy on the ethical use of AI among university students. A quantitative survey method was employed. Data were collected using a 1–5 Likert-scale questionnaire from 125 respondents, with 119 complete responses analyzed. Digital literacy was measured using 12 items, while ethical AI use was measured using 12 items. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity testing, reliability testing, correlation, and simple linear regression. The results show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI use. The correlation coefficient of 0.638 indicates a strong relationship, while the coefficient of determination of 0.406 indicates that digital literacy explains 40.6% of the variation in ethical AI use. The regression equation is Y = 1.196 + 0.706X. These findings indicate that students with higher digital literacy tend to use AI more ethically, responsibly, and transparently. This study recommends strengthening digital literacy programs with an emphasis on AI ethics in higher education.

items.title: Postgraduate Students' AI Engagement in L2 Academic Writing: Toward Student‐Led Human– AI Collaborations
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the teaching and learning of second language (L2) writing. Despite AI's affordances in assisting L2 writing, improvements in writing skills and learning outcomes that extend beyond producing polished texts largely depend on students' active AI engagement, typically involving AI‐generated content and AI tools. This study adopts a qualitative, classroom‐based inquiry to examine how 56 L2 postgraduate students engage with AI in an authentic academic writing class. Framing engagement as a multidimensional meta‐construct, we identify a contextualized pattern of engagement characterized by students' agential role in shaping human–AI interactions across behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions. Specifically, behavioral engagement occurs at compositional and operational levels, whereas cognitive engagement involves cognitive autonomy and metacognitive awareness. Students' emotional engagement involves appreciation and relief, as well as caution and emotional distance. Social engagement intersects with other dimensions, potentially shaping how students act, think, and feel in relation to AI through collaborative reflection. The findings inform a reconceptualization of engagement as a fluid, situated process, moving beyond a simple engagement–disengagement dichotomy toward a dynamic continuum shaped by the ongoing interplay across its multiple dimensions, encompassing both synergies and tensions. Implications for L2 writing and learning are also discussed.

items.title: Quantitative Study: The Effect of Digital Learning Media Interactivity on Children's Focus
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital learning media has intensified debate over which design characteristics most effectively support children's cognitive engagement. This study quantitatively examined the influence of digital learning media interactivity on children's learning focus, addressing a gap between the broader screen-time literature and the specific design features that shape sustained attention. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 116 elementary school-aged children (6-12 years) who regularly used digital learning media, selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using a validated and reliable structured questionnaire measuring digital learning media interactivity (navigation, responsiveness, feedback, interactive engagement, and learner control) and children's learning focus (selective attention, sustained attention, attentional control, and task engagement) on a five-point Likert scale, then analyzed using descriptive statistics, classical assumption testing, and simple linear regression in IBM SPSS Statistics. Both interactivity (M = 2.95, SD = 0.68) and learning focus (M = 2.95, SD = 0.67) were rated at moderate levels. Regression analysis showed that interactivity significantly and positively predicted learning focus (β = 0.469, t = 5.732, p < .001), with a moderate correlation (r = .473) and the model explaining 22.4% of the variance (R² = .224; F(1,114) = 32.857, p < .001). These findings indicate that interactivity is a meaningful, modifiable design characteristic that enhances children's attentional engagement, offering empirical guidance for teachers, parents, and developers in prioritizing interactive features over passive content delivery to support classroom attention.
